procedural_history.impugned_order: Award dated September 10, 1965, of the Labour Court, Jullundur in Reference No. 157 of 1959, directing reinstatement of Respondents 2 to 24 and holding the dismissal of Respondent No. 16 unjustified.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Respondents (presumably the workmen) filed a Writ Petition in the High Court of Punjab against the initial Award of the Labour Court. A Single Bench of the High Court held that the workers had not abandoned their services but that the management had terminated them and remanded the case to the Labour Court for a fresh decision. The management filed a Letters Patent Appeal against this decision but later withdrew it.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The management appealed to the Supreme Court by Special Leave against the Award dated 10-9-65 of the Labour Court after remand from the High Court.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal is accordingly allowed except for the Award m respect of Surat Singh, which is maintained.
directions: Having regard to the circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.

issue.issue_text: Whether the termination of employment of the Respondents in the circumstances of the case without an enquiry was justified.

facts: A group of workmen (the Respondents) went on strike after some of their co-workers were suspended.
The management and Labour Officers tried to persuade the striking workers to return to duty.
The workers refused to return unless the suspended workmen were also taken back.
The management sent notices giving the workers a deadline to rejoin, warning that their names would be removed from the muster roll if they failed to do so.
The workers did not respond and continued the strike, leading to the termination of their employment without a formal domestic inquiry.
The management conceded from the outset that the termination of one specific worker, Shri Surat Singh (Respondent No. 16), was invalid because there were no applicable standing orders for him.
law: Merely going on strike does not automatically justify the termination of an employee's services.
Generally, if an employee is accused of misconduct, the management must hold an inquiry, charge them with specific acts, and give them an opportunity to defend themselves.
However, even if no domestic inquiry is held by the management, the termination can still be justified if the management proves the misconduct with evidence before the Labour Court or Tribunal.

A persistent and obdurate refusal by workmen to join duty, after being given reasonable opportunities to do so, can constitute misconduct justifying termination, even without proof of other overt acts like violence or intimidation.
application: The Court first separated the case of Shri Surat Singh from the others. Based on the management's own concession, his termination was declared invalid, and his reinstatement was upheld.
For the remaining respondents, the Court found that although no domestic inquiry was held, the management had successfully justified its actions before the Labour Court.
The evidence showed that the management had made multiple attempts to get the workers to return and had given them over a month to do so.
The workers' continued refusal to work was deemed a "persistent and obdurate refusal" which constituted misconduct.
The Court rejected the argument that the management was acting under a pretext to deprive workers of benefits, noting that the notices gave them a clear opportunity to return to their jobs.
Therefore, the management had successfully proven the misconduct before the Labour Court, making the termination proper despite the lack of a prior internal inquiry.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided the issue partly in favor of the workers and partly in favor of the management. The termination of Shri Surat Singh was held to be unjustified because the management conceded it was invalid. However, the termination of the other respondents was held to be justified because, despite the absence of a domestic inquiry, the management successfully proved their misconduct (persistent refusal to work) with evidence before the Labour Court.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the termination of employment of the Respondents in the circumstances of the case without an enquiry was justified.
appellant_arguments: The management took every possible step to persuade the workmen to return to work, but they persistently and obdurately refused to do so, thereby abandoning their service.
The workmen engaged in an illegal strike.
The management was justified in striking the workmen's names off the muster roll due to their illegal activities and abandonment of service.
Given the circumstances, it was not necessary for the management to prove that the respondents were guilty of overt acts of intimidation, incitement, or violence.
respondent_arguments: The workmen did not abandon their services; rather, the management terminated their employment.
The termination of their services by the management was not justified.

cases.case_name: Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. v. Michael Mark & Anr.
cases.principle: If employees absent themselves from work because of a strike in enforcement of their demands, it cannot be considered an abandonment of employment. If the strike was illegal, the employer could take disciplinary action against the employees under the Standing Order.

cases.case_name: Punjab National Bank Ltd. v. Its Workmen
cases.principle: The jurisdiction of the Tribunal is not limited to an enquiry as to the contravention of Sec. 33 of the Act. Even if such contravention was proved, the employer could still justify the impugned dismissal on merits, and there is no difference in this regard between a reference under Sec. 10 of the Act and a dispute raised under Sec. 33A of the Act.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If management does not hold a domestic inquiry, it can still justify an order of termination before an industrial tribunal by producing satisfactory evidence of misconduct. Participation in an illegal strike, when coupled with a persistent and obdurate refusal by workmen to return to duty despite being given opportunities to do so, constitutes sufficient misconduct to justify termination without the need to prove additional overt acts of violence or intimidation.
obiter: It is an accepted principle of industrial adjudication that workmen can resort to a strike to press for their demands without snapping the employer-employee relationship.
Management has the right to carry on work during a strike, in furtherance of which it can employ other workmen and justify its action on merits in any subsequent adjudication.
The evidence required to justify action against workmen in an industrial adjudication is not as stringent as that which is required in a court of law.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: If management does not hold a domestic inquiry before terminating an employee, or if the inquiry held is invalid, the management can still justify the termination during industrial adjudication by producing satisfactory evidence before the Labour Court or Tribunal to prove the misconduct. The standard of evidence required in such a proceeding is not as stringent as in a formal court of law, but must be sufficient to satisfy the Tribunal that the termination was proper.
legal_tests_applied: In a dispute referred under Sec. 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, if management has not held a domestic inquiry or the inquiry is invalid, it can support its order of termination by producing satisfactory evidence and proving misconduct before the industrial adjudicator.

The evidence produced before the industrial adjudicator to justify the action taken against the workmen is not as stringent as that which is required in a Court of Law, but it should be such as would satisfy the Tribunal that the order of termination is proper.

While workmen can resort to a strike to press their demands without snapping the employer-employee relationship, the work of a factory cannot be paralysed by an illegal strike, and management has the right in those circumstances to carry on the work and justify its actions on the merits in a subsequent adjudication.

An industrial tribunal can interfere with the findings of a domestic inquiry only if there is mala fide, want of good faith, victimisation, unfair labour practice, basic errors, violation of principles of natural justice, or if the finding is completely baseless or perverse.
why_appellant_lost: The court's reasoning does not provide a basis for why the appellant's appeal was dismissed in respect of the workman Surat Singh, as the provided text focuses on the general principles justifying the termination of the other workmen.
why_respondent_won: The court affirmed the legal principle that the relationship of employer and employee does not automatically end simply because workmen go on strike.

The court established that management cannot terminate services merely on the ground that a strike is illegal; it must be shown through an inquiry (or later proof) that the conduct of the specific workmen amounted to misconduct.
policy_considerations: The court balances the right of workmen to strike in order to press for their demands against the right of management to prevent the factory's work from being paralysed and brought to a standstill by an illegal strike.

The court provides a procedural safeguard for management, allowing it to cure the defect of not holding a domestic inquiry by proving the misconduct with satisfactory evidence at the adjudication stage, thus prioritizing substantive justification over initial procedural formality.
